title: Draught-proofing: small gaps, big difference
description: Sealing the little gaps where cold air sneaks in is one of the cheapest ways to make a home feel warmer.

body.heading: Where draughts hide
paragraphs: Cold air finds its way in around front and back doors, sash windows, letterboxes, loft hatches, floorboard gaps and the holes where pipes and cables pass through walls. Each gap is small, but together they can swap the air in a room far faster than you would expect.
On a windy day, a slowly waved incense stick or the back of your hand near suspect edges will show you exactly where the leaks are. Mark them with sticky notes as you go.

body.heading: Simple fixes that work
paragraphs: Self-adhesive foam or rubber strips seal window and door frames; a brush strip or hinged flap tames a letterbox; a fabric draught excluder handles the gap under an internal door. Most of these cost little and need no tools beyond scissors.

Keyhole covers and a cap for an unused chimney are easy to forget and quick to fit. For floorboards and skirting, flexible filler made for the job lasts longer than ordinary sealant because it moves with the wood.

body.heading: Keep some air flowing
paragraphs: Draught-proofing targets uncontrolled leaks, not ventilation. Rooms with open fires, gas appliances or lots of steam, like bathrooms and kitchens, still need their vents and extractor fans working properly to avoid damp and keep air safe.

If condensation or mould appears after sealing up, that is a sign the room needs more deliberate ventilation, not that the draught-proofing was a mistake. Warmth and fresh air are both part of a healthy home.

takeaway: Find the gaps, seal them cheaply, and keep proper ventilation working where a room needs it.
